bodyText:
What is a Logic Gate?

A logic gate is an electronic circuit that performs a basic logical operation on one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output. Digital systems, from calculators to computers, are built entirely from combinations of gates. The behaviour of a gate is shown by its truth table, which lists the output for every possible input combination.

The Basic Gates

  • AND gate: the output is 1 only when all inputs are 1. Its Boolean expression is Y = A AND B.
  • OR gate: the output is 1 when at least one input is 1. Its expression is Y = A OR B.
  • NOT gate: also called an inverter, it has one input and reverses it: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.

The Universal and Special Gates

  • NAND gate: an AND gate followed by a NOT gate. Its output is 0 only when all inputs are 1.
  • NOR gate: an OR gate followed by a NOT gate. Its output is 1 only when all inputs are 0.
  • XOR gate (Exclusive OR): the output is 1 when the inputs are different.
  • XNOR gate: the output is 1 when the inputs are the same.

NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any other gate, and therefore any digital circuit, can be built using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

bodyText:
Boolean Algebra

Boolean algebra is the mathematics of binary values 0 and 1. It was developed by George Boole in 1854 in his book 'The Laws of Thought'. In 1938, Claude Shannon showed that Boolean algebra could describe telephone switching circuits, which founded the field of digital design. A Boolean expression uses variables, the operators AND, OR and NOT, and follows a set of laws that let expressions be simplified.

Fundamental Laws

  • Identity laws: A OR 0 = A, and A AND 1 = A.
  • Null laws: A OR 1 = 1, and A AND 0 = 0.
  • Idempotent laws: A OR A = A, and A AND A = A.
  • Complement laws: A OR NOT A = 1, and A AND NOT A = 0.
  • Double negation: NOT (NOT A) = A.
  • Commutative laws: A OR B = B OR A, and A AND B = B AND A.
  • Associative laws: grouping does not change the result.
  • Distributive laws: A AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C).
  • Absorption law: A OR (A AND B) = A.

De Morgan's Theorems

De Morgan's theorems, named after Augustus De Morgan, are the most used simplification rules. The first states that NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). The second states that NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B). In short, breaking a NOT over a bracket flips the operator between AND and OR.

Standard Forms

A sum-of-products (SOP) expression is a sum (OR) of product (AND) terms, for example AB + BC. A product-of-sums (POS) expression is a product of sum terms, for example (A + B)(B + C). Simplifying an expression reduces the number of gates needed to build the circuit.

bodyText:
What is a Karnaugh Map?

A Karnaugh map (K-map) is a graphical method for simplifying Boolean expressions. It was introduced by Maurice Karnaugh in 1953, based on the earlier Veitch diagram of 1952. Instead of applying laws step by step, the expression is plotted on a grid and simplified by grouping cells.

Structure of a K-Map

A K-map has one cell for every possible input combination. A 2-variable map has 4 cells, a 3-variable map has 8 cells, and a 4-variable map has 16 cells. The rows and columns are ordered in Gray code, so neighbouring cells differ in only one variable. Each cell corresponds to a minterm, numbered from m0 upward.

Rules for Grouping

  • Groups must contain 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells: only powers of two.
  • Groups must be rectangular and as large as possible, because larger groups give simpler expressions.
  • Groups may wrap around the edges of the map: the left edge is adjacent to the right edge, and the top to the bottom.
  • Every cell containing a 1 must be covered by at least one group, and groups may overlap.
  • Cells marked X are don't-care conditions: they may be treated as 0 or 1, whichever gives the simpler result.

K-maps are practical for up to about five or six variables; larger expressions are simplified by computer algorithms such as Quine-McCluskey.

bodyText:
What is a Combinational Circuit?

A combinational circuit is a digital circuit whose output depends only on the present inputs. It has no memory: it does not remember past inputs. Adders, multiplexers, decoders and encoders are all combinational circuits.

Adders

A half adder adds two single bits. It produces a Sum (A XOR B) and a Carry (A AND B). A full adder adds three bits: two input bits and a carry-in from a previous stage. It produces a Sum and a Carry-out, and it can be built from two half adders plus one OR gate. Full adders are chained together to build multi-bit adders, such as a 4-bit ripple-carry adder.

Multiplexers, Decoders and Encoders

A multiplexer (MUX), also called a data selector, selects one of many input lines and forwards it to a single output line. The selection is controlled by select lines: n select lines can choose among 2^n inputs, so a 4-to-1 multiplexer has two select lines. A demultiplexer does the reverse, sending one input to one of many outputs. A decoder converts n input lines into 2^n output lines, for example a 3-to-8 decoder has three inputs and eight outputs. An encoder performs the reverse operation, converting 2^n inputs into n outputs.

bodyText:
What is a Sequential Circuit?

A sequential circuit is a digital circuit whose output depends on the present inputs and on past inputs, because it contains memory elements. The memory elements are flip-flops, and the circuit's behaviour is synchronized by a clock signal.

Flip-Flops

A flip-flop is a one-bit memory cell. The main types are:

  • SR flip-flop (Set-Reset): S sets the output to 1 and R resets it to 0. The combination S = 1 and R = 1 is invalid because it gives an unpredictable result.
  • JK flip-flop: improves on SR by defining the previously invalid state: when J = 1 and K = 1, the output toggles.
  • D flip-flop (Data/Delay): the output follows the input D on the clock edge, so it stores one bit of data.
  • T flip-flop (Toggle): when T = 1 the output toggles on the clock edge, and when T = 0 it holds its state.

Registers and Counters

A register is a group of flip-flops that stores a multi-bit word: an n-bit register uses n flip-flops. A shift register moves bits left or right on each clock pulse, and comes in four forms: serial-in serial-out (SISO), serial-in parallel-out (SIPO), parallel-in serial-out (PISO) and parallel-in parallel-out (PIPO). A counter counts clock pulses. In a ripple (asynchronous) counter, flip-flops are triggered one after another, while in a synchronous counter all flip-flops receive the clock at the same time.
keyPoints: A sequential circuit's output depends on present inputs and past state.
A sequential circuit contains memory elements called flip-flops.

An n-bit register is made of n flip-flops.
